q: Translocation is the movement of dissolved substances through a plant.
e: Translocation specifically refers to the transport of organic solutes like sucrose and amino acids.

q: Water and dissolved salts from the soil travel downwards through the vessels of the xylem.
e: Water and dissolved salts travel upwards through the vessels of the xylem.

q: Food synthesized in the leaves passes downwards or upwards in the sieve tubes of the phloem.
e: Phloem transport is bidirectional, moving sugars to sinks both above and below the source.

q: Carbohydrates produced by leaves are transported out of the leaf in the form of sucrose to the stem.
e: Sucrose is the preferred transport sugar because it is highly soluble and metabolically stable.

q: Both upward and downward movement may take place at the same time in the phloem.
e: Different sieve tubes can transport materials in opposite directions simultaneously depending on source-sink relationships.

q: The phloem tissue is a complex tissue consisting of sieve tube, companion cell, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibre.
e: These four cell types work together to facilitate and support phloem transport.

q: All components of the phloem tissue are living cells including the phloem fibre.
e: They are living cells except for the phloem fibre, which is dead at maturity and provides structural support.

q: Sieve tubes or sieve cells have no nucleus and companion cells possess nuclei and work together.
e: The nucleated companion cell manages the metabolic needs of the enucleated sieve tube element.

q: Sieve cells can manage translocation without nuclei because they are kept alive by the nucleated companion cells.
e: Proteins and ATP required by the sieve tube are synthesized by the adjacent companion cell.

q: There are profuse cytoplasmic connections between sieve and companion cells.
e: Plasmodesmata connect the two cell types, allowing the transfer of nutrients and signaling molecules.
